Trademark & Sonic Architecture Explainer

The Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound™

The sonic architecture of absolute independence—and our open-culture guide to the difference between our proprietary brand mark (Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound™) and the public genre name anyone is free to use (80s Cosmic Pop).

1. Public Genre Name vs. Proprietary Trademark OPEN-CULTURE TRADEMARK POLICY

Under RaggieSoft Media's hybrid open-culture licensing model, creator Michael P. Ragsdale draws a clear, creator-friendly distinction between the generic musical genre (which belongs to everyone) and the specific brand trademark that identifies official RaggieSoft Media / Engine Room Records™ productions:

Free for Everyone to Use GENERIC GENRE NAME

"80s Cosmic Pop"

80s Cosmic Pop (along with descriptive terms like "Zero-G Synth-Pop" or "Cosmic Synth-Rock") is the generic, open sub-genre name describing an atmospheric blend of driving 1980s arena rock, gated percussion, fretless bass, lush analog synthesizers, and deep-space lyricism.

Public Usage Policy: Anyone—independent musicians, AI prompt engineers, music journalists, playlist curators, and fans—is 100% welcome and encouraged to call their own music, prompts, or playlists "80s Cosmic Pop" with zero restriction or attribution required.

Michael P. Ragsdale Trademark BRAND IDENTIFIER (™)

"The Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound™"

The Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound™ (and Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound™) is a proprietary common-law trademark claimed by Michael P. Ragsdale (doing business as RaggieSoft Media and Engine Room Records™) to designate authentic RaggieSoft audio releases engineered using our signature zero-gravity production architecture.

Brand Usage Policy: Please use The Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound™ only when referring to official recordings by The Stardust Engine™ / Engine Room Records™ (or in nominative fair-use commentary about RaggieSoft Media's work). When tagging or releasing your own non-RaggieSoft tracks in a similar style, please use the generic genre name "80s Cosmic Pop" instead.

In-Universe Origin (1987 → 1997 → 2011)

Within the narrative of The Stardust Engine, this zero-gravity sound is what Chief Audio Architect Cassidy O'Connell wanted to build in 1987—before Apex Records forced the band under a terrestrial "Plastic Sky" of safe corporate dance-pop.

Following the 1992 Friction emancipation, Cassidy finally realized the architecture on the five-part Cosmic Suite of Hard Reset (1997)—anchored by "Moon 1 (Tidal Lock)"—and expanded it into the low-sensory full-length haven Moon 1: Sanctuary (Zero-G) (2003). On October 18, 2011—the exact 25th Anniversary of "Ignition (The Forger's Call)" debuting inside The Crucible—the band released Starfield Calibration (2011), re-engineering 14 pre-2003 classics for both Cassidy's solo vocals and Ryan & Cassidy's sibling duets in pure zero-gravity.

In-Universe Legal Armor (Holly O'Connell)

Recognizing the value of her sister's phase-array synthesizer and spatial-reverb engineering, Manager and CEO Holly O'Connell immediately protected it inside the story world.

Through the independent boutique label she founded in 1992—Engine Room Records, LLC—Holly established the trademark to The Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound™ while gifting the generic genre name "80s Cosmic Pop" to the Ironheads and independent press. In-universe, when OmniCorp and Apex Records attempted to market knock-off "Tidal Lock" compilations in the late 1990s, Holly used that exact brand distinction to shut down their marketing campaigns overnight.

3. Archivist Note: The Suno AI Engineering Guide SUNO V5 / V6 VERIFIED

Because RaggieSoft Media shares our engineering workflows openly with the community, below are the exact Style Prompts and Cover Mode parameters used to generate tracks in this sonic architecture. Depending on the vocal arrangement, use crystal clear female vocals (for Cassidy's solo architecture) or male and female duet (for Ryan and Cassidy's sibling duets).

1. The Studio Master Prompt (Original Zero-G Tracks)

Use this for generating clean, original studio album tracks from scratch.

1980s synth-pop, mid-tempo space-rock, driving 4/4 gated drum beat, shimmering analog synthesizers, melodic fretless bassline, [crystal clear female vocals | male and female duet], lush spatial reverb, celestial atmosphere
2. The Starfield Calibration Cover & Lyrical Calibration Protocol (Suno v6)

Discovered by Michael P. Ragsdale while producing Starfield Calibration (2011) in Suno v6: when transposing an existing terrestrial rock, pop, or AOR song into Zero-G using Suno's Cover feature, you do not need to combine the original song's style prompt with the Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound™ prompt! Furthermore, the lyrics across Starfield Calibration were intentionally tweaked for two reasons:

  • Reason 1 — Celebrating Freedom from Apex Records (1987 Captivity → 2011 Orbital Freedom): Songs originally written under Apex Records' artificial "Plastic Sky" or on exhausting highway tours were updated from the perspective of nineteen years of independence, turning early cries of claustrophobia into retrospective celebrations of zero-gravity peace.
  • Reason 2 — Acoustic & Phonetic Vowel Extension for Zero-Gravity Reverb: The original terrestrial rock versions used clipped, percussive consonants to cut through distorted guitars and 130+ BPM arena drums. For The Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound™ (~100–118 BPM with wide spatial reverb and fretless bass), lines were tweaked to favor open, sustained vowels and liquid consonants ("gliding," "velvet," "alignment," "starlight," "zero-G," "tidal lock," "sanctuary") so the vocals hold long, shimmering legato notes that bloom inside the planetarium reverb tail.
  • Cover Audio Influence: Set to 74% (the exact sweet spot where Suno v6 locks onto the baseline melody, chord progressions, and vocal hooks—including call-and-response interplay—from the original audio, while giving the style engine room to rebuild the arrangement in Zero-G).
  • Style of Music Box: Include only the new Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound™ styles (do not paste the old terrestrial guitar/arena styles).
  • Exclude Styles (Negative Prompt): Explicitly strip away the original terrestrial instrumentation so Suno replaces it with phase-array synthesizers and fretless bass: heavy metal, grunge, acoustic folk, dry vocals, lo-fi, muddy mix, fast punk tempo, harsh distortion, screaming, shredding guitar solo
1980s synth-pop, mid-tempo space-rock, driving 4/4 gated drum beat, shimmering analog synthesizers, melodic fretless bassline, [crystal clear female vocals | male and female duet], lush spatial reverb, celestial atmosphere
3. The Live "Walk-On" Prompt (Act Opener)

Use this for the first song of a live set, or returning from an intermission. It allows Suno the freedom to generate a 60-to-90 second tension-building vamp in the dark before Cassidy starts singing.

  • Cover Settings: Audio Influence at 73%–74% | Weirdness at 0%
  • Lyrics Box Requirement: Top the lyrics with bracketed audio-environment tags like [Live Crowd Cheering] or [Low Synth Drone Intro].
1980s synth-pop, live stadium concert, massive crowd cheering, mid-tempo space-rock, driving 4/4 gated drum beat, shimmering analog synthesizers, melodic fretless bassline, [crystal clear female vocals | male and female duet], lush spatial reverb, celestial atmosphere, echoing stadium acoustics
4. The Live "Mid-Concert" Prompt (Immediate Start)

Use this for songs deep in the setlist where the momentum cannot stop. It mathematically forces Suno to skip the intro vamp and slam right into the track.

  • Cover Settings: Audio Influence at 73%–74% | Weirdness at 0%
  • Lyrics Box Requirement: Top the lyrics with bracketed hard-cues like [Continuous Crowd Roar], [Seamless Transition], and [Immediate Synth Riff].
1980s synth-pop, live stadium concert, massive crowd cheering, mid-tempo space-rock, driving 4/4 gated drum beat, shimmering analog synthesizers, melodic fretless bassline, [crystal clear female vocals | male and female duet], lush spatial reverb, celestial atmosphere, echoing stadium acoustics, mid-concert energy, seamless transition, continuous flow, immediate start
4. The Catalyst Track // Moon 1 (Tidal Lock) Hard Reset (1997) • Disc 2, Track 4

Moon 1 (Tidal Lock)

From Hard Reset (1997) • Disc 2: The Twin Moons • ISRC: QZTB92611796

Play "Moon 1 (Tidal Lock)" in The Listening Room Full Hard Reset Album
Lore Note: This track is unabashedly Cassidy’s favorite song on Hard Reset. It is a brilliant execution of pure, driving 1980s synth-pop, transposed entirely into the deep cosmos. Had Apex Records allowed them to write music this imaginative in 1987, this would have easily been the lead single on their debut. Lyrically, it uses the astrophysical concept of a "tidal lock"—where a moon is gravitationally bound to always show the exact same face to its planet—as a gorgeous metaphor for unwavering loyalty.
